title: The Fyre Fest of BookTok
content:

Over the weekend, hundreds of BookTok authors gathered in the Baltimore Convention Center for the Million Lives Book Festival. The event was billed as a magical weekend where readers could meet their favorite authors, especially romance and fantasy fiction authors who are popular on BookTok.

“Explore a vendor hall with authors from a wide range of genres, from fantasy and romance to mystery and dark romance,” the Eventbrite for the event read. “Engage in with other book lovers, attend insightful panels, and participate in our content creation room. This event will include a content creation room, fandom cosplay meet ups, a cosplay competition and a ball.”

What authors and fans were met with, however, was a massive and empty concrete hall with a bunch of foldable chairs inside and nothing else. There was seemingly zero promotion for the event, so authors were stuck hawking their books in empty hallways. The event apparently antagonized a disabled author for asking for basic ADA accommodations and exploited a pregnant author, who also took to TikTok to share her experience.

@azthiabookwyrmA Millon Lets Downs Book Festival.. The only good thing about this festival was the amazing people I was able to meet. Trauma bonding 🫶🫶 #booktok #booktokfyp #readersoftiktok #millionlivesbookfestival

Within minutes of the disaster, attendees began posting about it on TikTok. The videos across the platform detail what a clusterfuck the entire thing was from top to bottom. The organizer of the event issued a confusing, half hearted apology and promised refunds to those who reached out. However, so far no one who has reached out said they’ve gotten a refund. As of Monday morning Archer Management, who put on the festival, has been doing damage control in the event’s Facebook Group.

The Million Lives Book Festival is just the latest in a growing number of offline events that fail spectacularly to live up to online expectations. Social media has made it incredibly easy to market and promote events to niche internet communities, especially highly engaged ones like BookTok.

Share

With tools like Canva, AI-generated marketing copy, and scheduled content rollouts, the most barebones event can appear legitimate and exciting to people scrolling on social media. Hype cycles are then accelerated by influencers eager to be part of the next big event, and the aesthetics of an event often matter more than the logistics behind it. But the danger in this lies precisely in how easy it is to deceive.

Event organizers can mask their inexperience, lack of planning, or even outright grift behind a veneer of social media promo and the right branding. Of course, when the event actually arrives, the jig is up. But by then, organizers have usually collected the money.

The Million Lives Book Festival fiasco immediately reminded me of the AI-generated Willy Wonka Experience in Glasgow last February, where confused kids and their families were sent into a sparsely decorated warehouse lined with cheap props and actors performing AI-written scripts. These internet-fueled debacles like TanaCon and others, that show that virality and online hype are not a substitute for actual event planning. Fyre Festival, of course, is the most famous example of this disparity between social media and reality.

And yet, there's a bizarre lifecycle to internet failures. If they’re bad enough, the worst flops sometimes become cultural legends, ripe for a reboot. Ironically the terribleness of the event ends up bonding the actual community even tighter, setting the stage for a comeback.

Dashcon, once reduced to a punchline about a ball pit in the middle of a giant concrete room, is being revived in Canada by a team hoping to "do it right this time." Even Billy McFarland, the disgraced Fyre Festival founder, is promoting “Fyre Fest II” as a redemption arc.

Still, unless organizers of these internet IRL events begin to treat these communities with respect, transparency, and actual care, I think fandoms will soon tire of disasters like The Million Lives Book Festival. They will get burned out on over hyped experiences and I predict that event organizers will also face growing pressure to show their work in the planning stages. Funny memes and new friendships from a disastrous event only go so far when you’re out sometimes hundreds or thousands of dollars.
